newsitem.title: USA: Reuter survey projects steady economy through 1998.
newsitem.headline: Reuter survey projects steady economy through 1998.

text.p: Economic growth should slow over the next two years, helping to ease interest rates and keep inflation in check, a Reuters survey of 35 economists showed.
While no one in the quarterly survey forecast a recession, the experts did project a marked slowdown in the expansion rate of the economy.

On average, the economists estimated Gross Domestic Product grew at a 3.6 percent annual rate in the fourth quarter of 1996 but should slow to about 2 percent by the end of 1997. In mid-1998, GDP growth should bottom out at about 1.8 percent, those surveyed said.
"It's largely the business cycle," said Kim Rupert, senior economist at MMS International Inc., echoing the comments of several analysts. "The economy just eventually runs out of steam."
Chief among the factors expected to drain vitality from the economy will be a series of interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, some economists said.
While inflation should remain in check, near-term economic growth will be fast enough to push the Fed to raise short-term rates, said Steve Wood, managing director at BancAmerica Securities Inc.
"The economy is still outperforming their desires, (and) we're going to see the Fed finally act on this," Wood said.
The central bank's economic tuneup should brake some interest rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, cutting growth even further.
Long-term interest rates rose steadily over the past several weeks, and that should help get the slowdown in growth started.

Current interest rates "will cause housing, consumer durables and capital spending to slow even a bit more," said Donald Ratajczak, director of the Economic Forecasting Centre at Georgia State University.
A cooling economy eventually would ease inflation and long-term interest rates.
On average, the surveyed economists forecast the bellwether 30-year Treasury bond would yield 6.67 percent at the end of 1997 and 6.30 percent at the end of 1998.
The bond currently yields just below 6.9 percent.

Turning to inflation, the experts projected prices of most consumer goods, excluding food and energy, would grow about 3 percent a year in 1997 and 1998. Core consumer prices rose about 2 percent in the fourth quarter of 1996.
Many economists said the risk of somewhat higher inflation for the next two years comes from higher energy prices that are likely to trickle down into other consumer sectors.
"(Energy prices) are going to ... show up elsewhere in the economy," said David Blitzer, vice president and chief economist at Standard & Poor's Corp.
Demand for higher wages could also be a factor, he said.
"There are some areas out there where people are just going to want what they call their fair share of the pie," said Blitzer.
Many economists said the push for higher wages could be moderated if job insecurity continued, particularly if the unemployment rate were to creep up.

In a separate portion of the survey, economists projected the unemployment rate would rise only slightly to about 5.5 percent by fourth-quarter 1998 from about 5.25 percent during the current quarter.
A labour market operating at 5.5 percent unemployment coupled with inflation teetering near 3 percent would not throw the economy out of balance, economists said.

Thirty-five banks, securities firms and research institutions provided Reuters with forecasts for its latest quarterly survey of key economic indicators, interest rates and exchange rates. The survey was conducted from Jan. 21 through Jan. 23.
